item.title: Growing up in the South of England, like I did, history is all around you. Castles and forts, both preserved and ruined, litter the countryside. I, like many children, have fond memories visiting such places and imagining the great battles that were fought there. Read more
item.description:
Growing up in the South of England, like I did, history is all around you. Castles and forts, both preserved and ruined, litter the countryside. I, like many children, have fond memories visiting such places and imagining the great battles that were fought there.
All this came flooding back when I saw a hands-off demo of Chronicles Medieval recently at Gamescom. An upcoming action strategy game set within the Hundred Years' War that allows players to venture across Europe at a time when great armies fought fiercely over territory, it seemed immediately obvious to me it's the sort of thing that could only have been made by the most enthusiastic of history fans. And it turns out I was right.
Sam Millen, lead producer at Raw Power Games, as well as senior game designer Gareth Bourn, were keen to talk me through the upcoming release. "We have many members of the team who are history nerds," Millen explained when I asked about the amount of research needed to create Chronicles Medieval. The pair took great pride in scrolling across the game's rendition of Southern England, taking me to different towns and villages scattered across its landscape. These settlements are accurately placed based on where they would have been in real life, and their size likewise starts off at the scale they were at the time. There are 209 regions in total, with those yet undiscovered shrouded in a parchment-style fog of war.
Raw Power Games' eye for authenticity extends to Chronicles Medieval's battles. A knight's coat of arms matches that of their real-life counterparts, while the weapons they wield and the armour they wear are equally true to the time. I'm told the team worked with historians to get this right, and even have an in-house HEMA (historical european martial arts) expert.
This is all well and good, but previous games that have attempted to pay homage to real-world historical events have sometimes been so focused on authenticity, the fun factor has been lost in the process. Bourn describes this as a "fine balance to be struck", but believes the team has managed to strike it nonetheless.
"It's very important to make sure we're representing this time period accurately, so silly things like using a lance on foot aren't possible," he says. "So there are some limitations we've put in place to keep that authenticity alive, while stretching it to allow for more atypical choices that weren't necessarily prevalent."
Battles themselves play out as a blend of two genres: tactical strategy and third-person action RPG. You begin with a birds-eye view of the skirmish, able to place units freely within a starting section of the battlefield. You can also pre-programme manoeuvres that play out once the fight begins. In the demo I saw, for instance, cavalry were commanded to ride around the opposing army and flank them from behind.
Once this planning section ends, the action switches to third-person and you're placed in control of your player character. Here you can further command units within the slowed time, telling them to shift positions or raise their spears for incoming charges while the fight proceeds slowly around you. Then, once the action begins in earnest, you're able to take part personally. This could be holding out your weapon while riding your horse for fast-paced strikes, or getting off your horse entirely for more intimate brawls.
This, according to Millen, represents the duality of the commander in such battles. Real-world historical battles ultimately inspired the team at Raw Power who wanted the player to both command from a distance and get into the mud with their troops.
And progression in Chronicles Medieval further supports the fantasy of growing as a prominent commander. You start off bringing peasants and martial novices into battle with a few coins, and your own skills with weaponry and leadership are limited at first too. But, as you continue to win battles, your newfound knowledge of fighting provides new attacks you can personally use in combat, while units that survive multiple battles gain improvements to their cohesion - and their formations become tighter and increasingly effective.
One little feature I love, and that seems to perfectly encapsulate Chronicles Medieval's balance between historical accuracy and fun, is the impact of a cavalry charge, paired with a mechanic Millen calls "horse refusal". Here, a unit of knights on horseback carrying lances can, as you'd expect, cause significant damage. Once the charge is finished, though, they have to pull themselves and their steeds out of the mess of bodies and bloodshed to regroup and charge again. Exactly what you'd expect from a game aiming to provide that warring medieval fantasy.
But what about that "horse refusal"? Battle scholars and equidae experts note that, sometimes, your horse just doesn't fancy rushing into the fray. And so there's the ever-present possibility that one horse in a unit will pull away from the climactic clash - which can happen in-game. It's a little thing, but combined with myriad other small touches, it helps make Chronicles Medieval a rich playground for those looking for flavourful authenticity.
In Bourn's mind, it's these little details that make all the difference: "They're there because they're fun and they give advantages to the player, but if you're really into this stuff you'll be like, 'They refused, that's so cool!' You can see a reflection of how people have lived in the world before you arrive. Seeing cheap mercenaries have less cohesion than trained nobles, that's the sort of thing that brings life and colour to the world.
"It is a rich tapestry. The feudal system was deeply interesting in terms of vassals, barons, counts, dukes, and laws ... Reflecting all these things through systems and features just brings everything to life."

item.title: Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Kelsey takes solace in assassination; Connor revisits a foundational Korean MMO; Chris has some more thoughts about Marvel's Wolverine; Bertie tries to get to the end of Big Walk and then realises he doesn't want to get to the end of Big Walk at all; and Marie plays Spyro again, because why not? Read more
item.description:
Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Kelsey takes solace in assassination; Connor revisits a foundational Korean MMO; Chris has some more thoughts about Marvel's Wolverine; Bertie tries to get to the end of Big Walk and then realises he doesn't want to get to the end of Big Walk at all; and Marie plays Spyro again, because why not?
What have you been playing this week?
Here's another question: do you remember what you were playing last week? You don't have to! The What We've Been Playing archive has you covered.
It's been a whirlwind few weeks so I've decided to sit down with a comfort game of mine: Hitman World of Assassination. Don't ask me why I find stepping into the shoes of Agent 47 comforting, because I don't really know. I guess there's something about exploring the likes of Berlin, Dartmoor, and Hokkaido and looking for new assassination opportunities - like killing off corporate baddies with an explosive rubber duck and pretending you had nothing to do with it - that I find incredibly satisfying. I mean, that's no doubt what IOI was going for.
In preparation for the release of MapleStory Classic World - a revival of the original MapleStory from back in my childhood - I downloaded and booted up the modern iteration of the 2D Korean MMO.
I was totally lost. That game has truly evolved over the past decade or so, unsurprisingly. It was a strange feeling, like returning to your home town and realising that it's true, the world really does continue to change even when you're not there to see it happen.
I know it's most of what I write in these - I do promise I play more than just MMOs - but I admit it, I love the social aspect of these games, walking into a town and seeing people socialise, standing around in their shiny gear or with an especially big sword. Even a cursory adventure into Maplestory had me eager to play the Classic release this October. Thankfully there doesn't appear to be much else coming out that month, right?
This one's consumed my week, and so a few more quick thoughts on it beyond our review. One in particular is on the hand-holding, which has come up in other reviews and generally around the place since the embargo lifted. It is bad, no doubt about it. And generally speaking this stuff is rubbish and infantilising and a scourge on us all, etc, etc. There are times with Wolverine in particular where the amount of excessive signposting borders on parody. But to be contrarian (who, me?!) for a second: I don't think this is this game's biggest problem.
There is, I hate to admit, a place for this stuff sometimes. Wolverine is a brain-off linear game - a rollercoaster, as Scorsese once put it so perfectly when referring to the Marvel films. This is a Marvel movie in video game form if there ever was one. I don't think those movies are good, and I don't think Marvel's Wolverine is particularly good (Wolverine himself aside, who remains adorable). But there are far more egregious issues with it than letting me smash and slash my way through its Potemkin towns without also having to go through the great anguish of actually using my brain as well.
Back to it! The Eurogamer reader's game continues. Frankly I'm surprised we've managed to maintain interest for this long, with a week off while I reviewed Dawnwalker, and with some rehearsal clashes. A few originals couldn't make it but most were there, and a newcomer, which was nice. So, back in Bertie Land to see if we could get to the Big Walk endgame, which we couldn't, not quite - I blame the Asda delivery interruption. But I'm reminded now, while writing this, what a silly thing pushing for achievement is in a game like this.
That's not what this game is about. Big Walk is about creating space and time for other people, and experiencing things with them. That's right: it's a secret hippy retreat. And I'm reminded of this whenever something suboptimal happens, which is to say something that doesn't achieve a desired gaming end. It's getting lost together, it's writing silly slogans on signs for no apparent reason and then not being able to get through a doorway because you've got a noticeboard on your back. It's falling off the train and then trying to catch people as they jump back on, and failing, time and time again.
But there is pleasure in achieving - of course there is. Overcoming a tricky audio, gesture-related puzzle after what must have been 30 minutes of careful preparation was an incredible feeling - well done Dave! As was - and I loved this - discovering the most unexpected room deep underground in a tunnel system. Pushing for the finish line is contradictory to what this experience is. Indeed, I don't really want it to end.
If you fancy joining us, by the way, pop into the Eurogamer Discord and say so.
It was Spyro's birthday a few days ago - what better excuse to replay a game I've played numerous times before? And as much of a fan as I am of almost everything Spyro, I have an admission: I have never ever been able to master the flying levels, no matter how many attempts I make. Either in the original or as part of the Reignited Trilogy, I cannot get the timing right to pass the levels. They are the only thing standing in my way when it comes to 100 percent completing this game. Will I get there this time? That entirely depends on how patient I feel, and how many times I can bare to watch him crash into the water below after I misjudge the angle for flying through a time-boosting archway.

item.title: Last month, Sony argued that "reasonable consumers" already know they don't really own the digital goods they paid for. The Consumer Rights wiki has now made a list collecting more than 30 examples where Sony told customers they do, in fact, own the digital games they paid for. Read more
item.description:
Last month, Sony argued that "reasonable consumers" already know they don't really own the digital goods they paid for. The Consumer Rights wiki has now made a list collecting more than 30 examples where Sony told customers they do, in fact, own the digital games they paid for.
A class action lawsuit recently filed against Sony alleged the PlayStation Store isn't clear enough about the fact that digital purchases don't equal digital ownership. Once a player makes a purchase on the PlayStation Store, they're paying for a digital license that's revocable at any point in time - the purchase doesn't guarantee you'll have access to a particular game or DLC or cosmetic pack forever.
Sony's legal team fired back, arguing that it's not breaking any laws around digital ownership because "reasonable consumers would not be misled" by the storefront's small print disclosures. (You know, the links to the company's Terms of Service and Software Product Licensing Agreement that show up just before you pay for something on the PlayStation Store.)
Seemingly in response to those arguments, the Consumer Rights wiki has now created a "non-exhaustive table of references on Sony's site to 'owning' digital games." The list includes more than 30 occasions in which Sony's site has said something along the lines of, "View a broadcast for a game you own through the game's hub," or, "If you own the PS4 and PS5 versions of the same game, here's how to switch between them…"
One of the more recent examples can be found in Marvel's Wolverine's FAQ section: "Standard Edition owners can also upgrade to the Digital Deluxe Edition content."
The lawsuit claimants said Sony was in breach of a California Law that made it "unlawful for a seller of a digital good to advertise or offer for sale a digital good to a purchaser with the terms 'buy,' 'purchase,' or any other term which a reasonable person would understand to confer an unrestricted ownership interest in the digital good." (Reasonability doesn't seem like something you could measure in court, but I digress.) A digital vendor can get around the law by giving customers clear information about the licenses they're paying for. We'll see how the suit plays out over the coming weeks and months.

item.title: Physical versions of Final Fantasy 7 Revelation require a download anyway because Square Enix would've had to compromise the game in some fashion to contain the entire mammoth adventure in a disc. At least, that's the reasoning series director Naoki Hamaguchi has given. Read more
item.description:
Physical versions of Final Fantasy 7 Revelation require a download anyway because Square Enix would've had to compromise the game in some fashion to contain the entire mammoth adventure in a disc. At least, that's the reasoning series director Naoki Hamaguchi has given.
Anyone sitting in the venn diagram middle of Final Fantasy 7 fan and physical games collector might have gone from extremely happy to kinda bummed earlier this week. The third and final part of the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy is shipping in a physical format on all three major consoles (hurray), but you'll still need to download additional game data to get going.
"Each platform has limitations when it comes to physical media capacity, but we believed that compromising the quality of the final chapter in order to achieve a fully on-disc release would ultimately not be in the best interest of many fans," said Remake trilogy director Naoki Hamaguchi in an online statement.
"We understand that this decision may not meet everyone's expectations. Even so, in today's market, where the industry is steadily moving toward a disc-less future, we believe there is real value in being able to offer a physical edition at all," he added.
Fans have since put forth their own online counters, pointing out that both Final Fantasy 7 Remake and Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth launched on two discs that together contained the entire game. Theoretically, Square Enix could've repeated the trick a third time and had Final Fantasy 7 Revelation come out with multiple discs stuffed into a plastic package.
As it stands now, physical PS5 and Xbox Series X boxes include one disc, while Nintendo Switch 2 copies contain a controversial Game-Key card - all three require an internet connection for an extra install.
Physical releases have been a hot topic ever since Sony announced plans to stop manufacturing new PlayStation games on discs starting in 2028. That PR disaster persisted through the entire summer and is still chomping at Sony's heels, if reactions to the company's recent State of Play show were any indication.

item.title: Players cancelling their subscriptions to video game services like Xbox Game Pass and PlayStation Plus are more likely to blame costs today than they were at the start of the year. Read more
item.description:
Players cancelling their subscriptions to video game services like Xbox Game Pass and PlayStation Plus are more likely to blame costs today than they were at the start of the year.
That's according to new data shared by Circana's senior director and video game analyst Mat Piscatella, who explained that more people are being pushed out of monthly video game subscriptions due to costs, at least, in the US.
"According to Circana's Future of Insights for Video Games Consumer Survey, cost is becoming a stronger driver of US cancellations to Xbox Game Pass Essential, PS Plus Essential and Nintendo Switch Online," Piscatella said on BlueSky. "Over 40% of those canceling in the US cite cost as a primary driver, higher than seen in Q1."
Piscatella is quick to note this data doesn't indicate that more people are cancelling video game subscriptions. "It has no relation to the number of people canceling," he wrote. It's just that the people who have given up on memberships are more likely to point the finger at costs instead of, let's say, a weak selection of games.
In Circana's latest survey, 50% of people who cancelled their Nintendo Switch Online membership over the last few months chose the option that read, "Couldn't justify the cost of the subscription within my budget but liked the service." That number was 40% earlier in the year. For Xbox Game Pass Essential and PS Plus Essential, 40% of cancellers gave the same reason compared to 37% in Q1.
The news is perhaps unsurprising since almost everything else in the gaming world, from hardware to the games themselves, have only become pricier in recent times. PS Plus saw a price hike just earlier this year, while Xbox Game Pass subscriptions almost doubled until the company reversed course and decoupled Call of Duty from the service. The only one to weather the storm has been Nintendo Switch Online, which has stayed the same price in most regions.
All three major consoles have also been subject to price bumps this year due to vague "market conditions" - or, if you're reading between the lines, AI data centres sucking up memory components and sending costs rocketing for other hardware manufacturers.

item.title: It's science-fiction Friday as Google's fully mapped fly brain, which was revealed last week, has been engineered to play Doom and rhythm-action game Beat Saber. Read more
item.description:
It's science-fiction Friday as Google's fully mapped fly brain, which was revealed last week, has been engineered to play Doom and rhythm-action game Beat Saber.
Google's brain-mapping is a historic first and the model of the fly brain - which took years of work and AI-help to compile - was released by the company's research team and made available for download. A few days later, as reported by PC Gamer, this resulted in the brain being trained to play Doom.
the fly brain can play doom pic.twitter.com/aTYBOd868m
"I'm training a fly brain to play Doom using the full MaleCNS v1.0 fruit fly connectome," announced Coinbase engineer Alex Wormuth, who also published a live video feed of the simulated fly's progress. Apparently it played thousands of times and is still not doing very well.
Not long after, another enterprising engineer, domi on Bluesky, got the fly brain playing lightsaber-based rhythm-action game Beat Saber. A video shows a little fly model waving the lightsabers around and slicing through advancing tiles, probably better than I would.
The same modder got the fly brain playing shooters, using the fly's brain to work out when to turn, apparently, and its "courtship song" for when to shoot. "The more aroused the fly is the harder it tries to shoot," domi noted, alarmingly.
Google had already successfully mapped the brain of a female adult fruit fly, but this time it's a male fruit fly's brain that's been mapped - and as Google pointed out, there's a notable difference. "It's a big step in advancing neuroscience experiments", Google said, perhaps envisioning it running on Doom, "and promises to be a foundational resource for neuroscience for years to come".

item.title: Following Sony's announcement earlier this week that it had "stepped away" from Kojima Production's previously PlayStation-exclusive "action espionage" Physint, a new report has claimed Sony's decision was the result of concerns over "budget, potential profitability and exclusivity." item.description:
Following Sony's announcement earlier this week that it had "stepped away" from Kojima Production's previously PlayStation-exclusive "action espionage" Physint, a new report has claimed Sony's decision was the result of concerns over "budget, potential profitability and exclusivity."
Speaking to Bloomberg, sources familiar with the project said a major factor behind the decision was the commercial performance of Hidea Kojima's prior two games, Death Stranding and Death Stranding 2. While both were critically acclaimed, they reportedly did not pull in the revenue Sony expected.
It's also claimed Physint was over budget, and had missed deadlines despite "being years away from release." The game was also set to be published on other platforms aside from the PlayStation, and Sony was "reluctant" to invest hundreds of millions of dollars into a project that wouldn't be exclusive to its console ecosystem.
This follows reports earlier this year that Sony has abandoned its previous multi-format approach, and would no longer release its single-player PlayStation games on PC, instead keeping them PS5-exclusive. Physint, as an IP owned by Kojima Productions, would have run against this strategy. Bloomberg also notes that while Hideo Kojima and Sony have had a tight business relationship for decades, the PlayStation executives close to Kojima have left in recent years.
Sony has also faced significant software-related troubles in recent years, including 2024's Concord flop and Marathon's continued struggles, which has led the company to implement stricter production milestones, according to Bloomberg. This, in turn, has resulted in several game cancellations.
Additionally, Bloomberg notes the hardware cost crisis caused by the generative AI industry has made consoles more expensive, both for consumers to buy and for Sony to produce. As a result, the company is now focused on maximising revenue from its existing userbase, rather than pushing to grow its audience.
Enter Xbox, which swooped in to pick up Physint following Sony's departure from the project. Microsoft's gaming arm has struggled with its own share of controversies in recent times, including sweeping layoffs and the ongoing impact of BDS boycotts.
According to Bloomberg, Physint was seen as a good investment by Xbox due to its presence on PC, and its film and television rights, which aligns with prior statements from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma on pushing the company's franchises into different mediums.
An Xbox spokesperson even provided Bloomberg a statement when asked, saying, "Betting on Kojima-san is an easy call. We believe in his team’s ability to build AAA games with groundbreaking, new IP and we believe in OD, Physint, and our growing partnership."

item.title: Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) is reportedly considering combining EA - which it acquired in a $55bn leveraged buyout earlier this year - with its Savvy Games Group, all under one banner. Read more
item.description:
Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) is reportedly considering combining EA - which it acquired in a $55bn leveraged buyout earlier this year - with its Savvy Games Group, all under one banner.
Speaking to Bloomberg, unnamed sources familiar to the matter claimed the merger between the EA and Savvy Gaming Group is intended to "ensure better coordination between its assets". This comes roughly two months after the record-breaking leveraged buyout of EA was finally finalised, placing the creator of EA FC, Apex Legends, Battlefield 6, and more under new ownership.
Savvy Games Group is a PIF subsidiary that already owns Scopely (creator of Pokémon Go) and various esports companies like ESL, as well as a variety of partial stakes in Capcom, Nintendo, Koei Tecmo, and others. It has been the spearhead of Saudi Arabia's expansion into the video game industry for many years, but was notably not used to buy out EA earlier this year.
Last week, the CEO of Savvy Games Group, Brian Ward, stepped down from his role. He oversaw many of Savvy's massive acquisitions and investments over the past few years, and his departure looks increasingly interesting given this new report.
What the future looks like for EA following its acquisition has been the focus of much discussion. Some experts believe the nature of the leveraged buyout, and the substantial amount of debt EA now has to pay off annually, could result in EA abandoning its single-player portfolio and cutting staff.

item.title: Rockstar Games and the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) have traded blows in fiery opening statements during the final employment tribunal hearing, relating to the sudden firing of 31 Rockstar North employees nearly a year ago. Read more
item.description:
Rockstar Games and the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) have traded blows in fiery opening statements during the final employment tribunal hearing, relating to the sudden firing of 31 Rockstar North employees nearly a year ago.
In their opening statements - made as the hearing got underway in Glasgow, Scotland, yesterday, and shared in full with Eurogamer - the opposing organisations outlined a case hinging on a private IWGB Discord server and what was and wasn't talked about there. It's on this Discord server that hundreds of Rockstar employees hoped to organise and create a legally recognised Rockstar union, but it's also here that Rockstar alleged confidential information was disclosed.
The 31 fired Rockstar North employees, represented by the IWGB, claimed Rockstar was "clandestinely monitoring" this Discord server through a "mole" since "at least" February 2024, but that Rockstar only took punitive action days after membership numbers reached the pivotal 10 percent figure (of a larger workforce) needed for unions to be recognised by UK law.
In the IWGB's opening statement, it said: "[Rockstar] asks the Tribunal to accept that, after monitoring the Server for almost two years without taking any disciplinary action, it happened to discover misconduct requiring the [former employees'] immediate dismissal fortuitously at exactly the moment when the union had acquired the capacity to seek recognition. The [former employees] say that the contemporaneous evidence points to a much simpler, realistic and credible explanation: [Rockstar] struck at the union because it had become capable of exercising collective power."
The IWGB statement documented dozens of alleged meetings between Rockstar's cyber security person and the "mole" over 21 months, with a drastic uptick in activity around October 2025, as the 10 percent threshold was reached. It claimed that "much of the union's organising cadre" was targeted by Rockstar in the resulting "decimation", and that those employees - which were invited to brief "catch-up meetings" by Rockstar - were handed pre-prepared dismissal letters and escorted from their workplace with no discussion or opportunity to defend themselves.
Rockstar, naturally, disagreed. Much of its case seemed to rest on having the tribunal understand what it called the "embedded culture of confidentiality" it operates with, as well as the "exceptional value and prestige" of Grand Theft Auto 6. Rockstar said it adopts "the security posture of a Wall Street Bank" to guard its secrets in the way Coca-Cola would its secret "formula" or Apple would its technology.
Accordingly, Rockstar said any visitors to its offices "must" sign NDAs and that any contractors on site are escorted by security. Remote working is "severely restricted", external storage devices are "banned", photography is "strictly forbidden", and personal phones, tablets, and laptops are "blocked" from connecting to Rockstar systems.
Rockstar claimed it sustains "regular assaults on its security and systems" and that "it has had to put privacy films on its building after drones were used to try and photograph through office windows". It also cited an alleged phishing attack that supposedly resulted in "dozens of videos of unfinished development footage of GTA 6" leaking onto Slack in 2022. As a result, the company said it employs a full-time team of five investigators and a director "to monitor for and investigate potential data leaks".
Rockstar mentioned the recent Cyberleek GTA 6 video leaks, too: "Most recently, in the last few weeks, a hacking group attempted to blackmail [Rockstar]. If any more proof was needed that [Rockstar's] sensitivity to security and confidentiality is justified, it is the wiping of $2bn from the [Rockstar's] parent company's share value within a few days as that recent hack became public."
Hunger for information on GTA 6 is so great, Rockstar claimed, it faces "levels of scrutiny that are hard to conceive". It alleged to have had "the frequency of coffee shop trips by employees and pizza deliveries to the Rockstar offices" monitored by outside parties, presumably in the hope of their gleaning any information about what was going on inside. In 2023, a "return to office" plan leaked and apparently "generated global coverage and spin-off theories about what this might mean for the release date of GTA 6".
With this in mind, Rockstar said it was moved to take action when "whistleblowers" within the IWGB Discord - who it claimed had sent only "snippets" of information since 2023 - became "so alarmed" with what they saw they contacted the company. Rockstar then apparently gained access to the Discord and when it saw what was going on, took action. This is its account of the sudden urgency scrutinised by the IWGB.
Rockstar claimed that upon accessing the Discord server, it discovered a journalist there, as well as former employees which it said "left in poor standing with the business and were therefore motivated to cause harm to it". However, the IWGB maintained that the Discord servers were invite-only, access-restricted and "subject to verification through Rockstar's own internal Slack platform", and only used to discuss union-related issues like meetings, training, surveys, petitions, collective responses, advice, and representation. The biggest Discord room apparently had nearly 350 people in it - both parties agree on this.
Rockstar also alleged it found "vituperatively disparaging" remarks about the company on Discord server, in phrases such as "cowardly corporate fucks", and words like "arseholes", "narcissistic", "abusive", and "bastards". More importantly, it allegedly found references to game features there - "one of the most closely guarded secrets of the company". "Two discussed an online 32 player format which was highly confidential at that time," Rockstar said, and people were allegedly spotted speculating about a release delay to Autumn 2026 long before that was officially announced.
Rockstar concluded: "There can only be one sole or principal reason for dismissal. [Rockstar] says, very simply, the reason for the dismissals was the misconduct which it uncovered on the Discord which led to an irretrievable breakdown in trust and confidence.
"If, as the [former employees] claim, [Rockstar] was hostile towards the IWGB and had been since 2023, and was fearful of it achieving the 10 percent recognition threshold, it would have been insanity itself for the Respondent to take no action until the IWGB had already reached that threshold, and then in a 48 hour period simultaneously sack 31 union members. Their case is – literally – incredible."
Yesterday's employment tribunal hearing was accompanied by rallies and placards as some of the people fired by Rockstar gathered outside. In an impassioned speech, one former worker characterised the battle against Rockstar as being a battle against a fear itself. "Fear wants to rule us," they said. "It closes our minds, our hearts, and our horizons. It makes us small, sad and hopeless. But today, we are fighting fear. This long-awaited hearing is an opportunity to put fear in its place below us."
The tribunal hearing is expected to last five weeks as the submitted evidence is discussed and cross-examined. It is a landmark case for video game union representation whatever the outcome - not least for reaching as far as UK Parliament - but should the tribunal rule in favour of the fired employees, it will be an historic victory. We'll keep you posted on the ins and outs of the hearing over the coming weeks.

item.title: The City of Miami Beach has approved negotiations with Rockstar Games for an upcoming marketing campaign. This would bring advertisements for Grand Theft Auto 6 to the seaside city in exchange for millions of dollars. Read more
item.description:
The votes came in at 4-3, following arguments between those concerned with the violent nature of the game and others seeing value in the promotional power of Rockstar's upcoming mega-release. Through this debate some components of the deal being negotiated were disclosed by commissioner Laura Dominguez.
This includes the current price Rockstar is expected to pay, which is $3m. However, Dominguez noted the city would attempt to negotiate for a higher fee. Later in the meeting, commissioner Tanya Katzoff Bhatt indicated the city would receive benefits "closer to $4m". GTA6 would be advertised "discreetly" through Boucher Brothers beach chairs and umbrellas, featuring the roman numerals VI or Vice City rather than the words Grand Theft Auto.
This campaign is currently planned to run from the 15th October through to the end of the year. However, it will not be advertised at Miami Beach's Art Basel event in early December. Also, these GTA adverts won't be present on city property, including iconic landmarks or lifeguard stands.
This approval was far from a sure thing, with some commissioners sharing their displeasure with the GTA series and its depiction of violence. Commissioner David Suarez presented video footage of both GTA5 and the recent GTA6 extended preview on Netflix. While showing the police car chase during the extended preview, Suarez said: "I certainly don't want to see our brand associated with this video game, I don't think it's worth any amount of money."
That money, however, would be incredibly valuable to the city, others argued. Commissioner Bhatt said: "This is coming to Miami Beach with or without us, and to pretend that it isn't is a missed opportunity [...] "It's actually close to $4m or so in benefits to the city, which itself would pay for the Flamingo football field renovation project that is currently not funded, which is of vital importance to families all across the city."
This debate has raged far beyond the city commission meeting. Miami-Dade county sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz spoke out about the planned promotion between the city and Grand Theft Auto 6, saying: "Grand Theft Auto is a video game franchise built around criminal activity — we need to seriously consider the message we send when our own government promotes a fictional identity centered around many of those same crimes."

item.title: Spanish studio MercurySteam - the developer of Metroid Dread - seems to be the studio behind yesterday's Nintendo Direct showcase stopper, Metroid Ravenous. Read more
item.description:
Spanish studio MercurySteam - the developer of Metroid Dread - seems to be the studio behind yesterday's Nintendo Direct showcase stopper, Metroid Ravenous.
Questions were raised after the Direct showcase because, despite the obvious visual similarities between Metroid Dread and Ravenous, MercurySteam's name did not appear in the Ravenous trailer or on any associated press gumpf. MercurySteam's social accounts were also quiet following the event.
I sought clarification from Nintendo and from MercurySteam this morning because of this, but heard nothing back - though this silence is not unusual for Nintendo, which often doesn't disclose developers until close to a game's release.
Nonetheless, MercurySteam appears to have ended speculation today by retweeting yesterday's Metroid Ravenous trailer with a ninja emoji and a heart emoji, presumably signalling some kind of stealth development situation. The same trailer was shared on LinkedIn by the company moments ago as well.
Metroid Ravenous seems to closely follow the Metroid Dread template, offering a side-on Metroid adventure, albeit one that plays with perspective a lot. Ravenous appears more colourful and less oppressive than Dread, and its montage of energetic gameplay lit-up Nintendo's Direct yesterday afternoon.
2021's Metroid Dread scored a golden Essential badge in Eurogamer's review, with Martin Robinson calling it "a stylish, visually sumptuous return for 2D Metroid, and an adventure that proudly sits alongside the series' best".
Since then, MercurySteam - known for the Castlevania Lords of Shadow games - worked on an original game idea called Blades of Fire, which reviewed pretty well, but ultimately "underperformed", putting financial pressure on the company that forced restructuring and layoffs a couple of months ago. It's good to see the studio back in action again.
Metroid Ravenous is being released exclusively for Switch 2 on 28th January 2027.

item.title: Nintendo of America is currently facing a class action lawsuit for refusing to pass tariff refunds onto customers, and it's against that backdrop it today announced a "Customer Appreciation Sale" apparently made possible by those rebates. Read more
item.description:
Nintendo of America is currently facing a class action lawsuit for refusing to pass tariff refunds onto customers, and it's against that backdrop it today announced a "Customer Appreciation Sale" apparently made possible by those rebates.
In a blog post, Nintendo called this one of its "largest promotions ever", and included the following line which has had people scratching their heads: "While Nintendo absorbed most tariff-related costs, the refunds helped make promotions like this one possible."
A quick recap: following the introduction of tariffs by the current US government last year, Nintendo increased the price of multiple products in the country, citing "market conditions" as justification.
Nintendo, in this sale announcement, argues that it "absorbed" most of the costs, but the company has received a refund. The US consumers who bought Nintendo products since the price increase also suffered increased costs thanks to the tariffs, but they aren't receiving refunds. The reason this is rubbing people the wrong way is because Nintendo is thanking them for dealing with increased costs by encouraging them to spend more money.
The counter argument is, hey, why look a gift horse in the mouth? This is a discount on some games and peripherals at a time when buying new stuff in this market is awfully expensive. This ultimately could be seen as a gesture of goodwill, and one Switch owners could benefit from.
The reaction to this sale has, as you can imagine, resulted in some interesting reactions online. You can find a few of them below:
"The Customer Appreciation Sale... is made possible in part by tariff-related refunds. While Nintendo absorbed most tariff-related costs, the refunds helped make promotions like this one possible." That's.... not how sales work. Such odd framing.[image or embed]
"To claim your tariff-related refund, please give us more money" https://t.co/punlfKv5St
I guess I shouldn't look a gift horse in the mouth but if this is because of the tariff refund like the post says, why not just... permanently lower the price on some of this stuff? No? No?[image or embed]
Nintendo is also currently pushing back against a class action lawsuit that it has no obligation to pass on refunds onto its customers, arguing that Switch buyers got "what they bargained and paid for". Microsoft and Sony are joining Nintendo, arguing against tariff refunds along similar lines.
This sale is set to run from the 13th September to the 26th September on the Nintendo eShop, Nintendo Store, and participating retailers. Nintendo would like to say thank you, but not for too long.

item.title: I've always thought there were a few characters out there who were the perfect match for video games. Batman is always my classic example: he beats up bad guys, does stealth takedowns, and has a built-in arsenal of gadgets that can be conveniently designed for any design obstacle; he has a cool car and cape for driving and/or gliding around an open world, and he has preternatural detective sensibilities to help him solve environmental puzzles - or, I dunno, press R3 to see where to go next. item.description:
I've always thought there were a few characters out there who were the perfect match for video games. Batman is always my classic example: he beats up bad guys, does stealth takedowns, and has a built-in arsenal of gadgets that can be conveniently designed for any design obstacle; he has a cool car and cape for driving and/or gliding around an open world, and he has preternatural detective sensibilities to help him solve environmental puzzles - or, I dunno, press R3 to see where to go next.
You can say the same for Spider-Man, I think, plus the Jedi - and Bond, of course, was another who finally got the typical action game protagonist revamp earlier this year. But the last, really obvious one to be modernised, to me, has been Wolverine. He has the combat skills down pat, and a nice diegetic reason to be able to infinitely heal his wounds and sniff out the way to the next objective or erstwhile collectible. He can scarper up walls and jump extra far. But he also goes a bit beyond the standard action stuff, because in many ways Wolverine is a perfect fit for what's become the de facto modern day, western "prestige" triple-A gaming protagonist: a gruff, traumatised, middle-aged guy with a layer of molten tragedy beneath his crusty, battle-worn outer surface, ready to occasionally burst forth into a fountain of ultra-violent rage. Typically when you've hit lots of guys and then press two buttons together.
If you're much like me you might feel this sort of thing is starting to get a bit overdone - especially within PlayStation's first-party offerings, which, as I've written before, have all started to merge into one. Count how many Sony-developed games in the past five years have grapple hooks, climbable ledges, parries, gliders, RPG-lite skill trees, waist-high grass, ultra-simple environmental puzzles, and a form of rage meter that fills up until you can press L3+R3 or L2+R2 for an ultimate of some kind, and the formula doesn't so much reveal itself as it does write it on your forehead in yellow paint.
Usually these all play out in a variation on the not-quite-open-world format, and for the longest time Marvel's Wolverine was assumed to be another in the same mould. But to its benefit, it's a little different - only a little, admittedly, as it does have about half of those things. And crucially, I need to add a big point of emphasis here as well: all these things, while never remotely groundbreaking, can still be very, very good fun. I'm a sucker for big, punch-powered bombast when the developers get it right, and especially so for weaving these more familiar mechanics into something new and spectacular (see: Returnal).
One of those points of difference is not to its benefit, despite the potential. Wolverine's linear format, which could have been so refreshing, offering a chance for compactness and concentrated highlights, does nothing to prevent it becoming a repetitive, overlong and overfamiliar slog. But the other big one is: Wolverine, despite being perhaps the one, true sad-but-tough middle-aged protago-dude to end them all, is in fact here characterised entirely differently to what you might expect. This Wolverine is openly vulnerable, emotive, apologetic, kind. He's a straight up action hero, despite his own protestations, and a totally charming one.
This not-what-you-might-expect vibe is matched by the narrative setup. There are no X-Men in Marvel's Wolverine's universe (or at least no team by that name), and instead we're dropped into the action with Logan as a member of Team X, a deeper cut from the comics. Even that team has had a reworking, too: rather than the government unit it is there, Team X is here run by Nathanial Essex, a mysterious psychic-powered man from the 1800s (voiced and mo-capped by Troy Baker, with an enjoyably arch English accent). He's also set up a kind of refuge-slash-base for the team called the Essex Institute, with the team finding and rescuing the increasingly scarce mutants of the world to offer them refuge, leading to the overall sense this is more of an alt-universe X-Men than something where they may someday appear.
Despite the deviation from any specific comic story, if you're heavily plugged into them you'll know where this goes - and frankly even if you're only lightly aware of X-Men storylines you'll be able to predict each turn long before it happens. The storytelling in Marvel's Wolverine is broad and obvious - the theme of found family and resistance against the militarised rounding-up of minorities is present and correct, as it should be for an X-Men-adjacent story. (The upside of this is some especially satisfying skull-mashing; the downside that none of it is exactly subtle.)
But then at the same time, the initial drop into the action will be disorientating for the vast majority of players who broadly know Wolverine from, say, the main X-Men films and their hazy memories of the 90s cartoon. The amount of exposition everyone needs to get through, and the fact we open somewhat in media res, with a bombastic tutorial level that's actually Wolverine's return to the team he'd apparently previously left, even though the player never saw Wolverine anywhere but firmly in the team, feels a little back to front.
This is a minor thing but it's actually a symbol of something wider I found with Marvel's Wolverine's story: a lot of the great character work is happening off-screen. There's little of the usual soul-searching, small town Americana Logan you might've expected - especially from that barroom tease that revealed the game (which never happens in it, by the way) - and as a result, it can feel like Wolverine's something of a passenger in his own story. The first third of the game is essentially just order-following for Essex, and all the key events that follow simply cascade down from doing stuff because that's what happened to need doing at the time.
You kind of want to recall some lost memories, for instance, but also maybe you don't, and that's ratified by the game in the form of Nightmare Doors - optional, minutes-long challenges and time trials you can do to unlock a brief verbal recollection of a vague past. Their optionality is symbolic of how secondary this feels to Logan himself. To put it in totally insufferable armchair writer terms: it feels a little like Logan's a character without a clear motivation. He's dragged through the story by the nose (often literally, given the whole smell thing), rather than propelling himself - and you - forward through a clear desire of his own. There's a way to do this sort of thing, where you make the lack of direction the point, an existential quest to find purpose and meaning, but that's not it either. It's all pretty disappointing, given how central things like a quest for identity or the overcoming of inner demons are to this character by default. The story's right there for the taking. Instead, Logan's famed memory loss is a plot device rather than a character-making one, and Wolverine's just caught up in some villains' villaining - and now several thousand people must be stabbed.
The flipside to all this however is that Wolverine himself, the way the character's written and animated by developer Insomniac, and performed with a kind of enchanting, puppy-dog innocence by actor Liam McIntyre, will totally win you over. This Logan has sad eyes and a big smile. He drops a few good one-liners, in addition to the air-punching moments and expected catchphrases. This is very much the lying in bed, staring forlornly at a little picture frame Wolverine, though because he can't remember anything of consequence here the picture is presumably of a bottle of whiskey or maybe a cool motorbike. This Logan kisses, hugs, rests his head on shoulders, role-plays as a cartoon cat-pirate for kids, rescues people because he cares about them, or sometimes just because it's the right thing to do.
That disarming tenderness extends to the rest of the cast as well. Sabretooth, Logan's best friend-slash-nemesis, seems only capable of talking in caps lock and has all the prerequisite violence and comedy brutishness, but in one fateful moment late on reveals himself as also something of a pussycat. Mystique is another wounded animal, lashing out viciously but often only out of an overabundance of love. Even Essex is chillingly accomplished at the gentle, crocodile teared non-apology. The only slight disappointment is Jean Grey, who's performed perfectly well by Krizia Bajos, but given a bit of a dud hand here, written as a little excessively doting, and too often relegated to the role of door-opening, platform-lifting accomplice who could have easily had her own story brought much more to the fore.
The action, after all that, is similarly so-so. The rundown will sound familiar: you can slash with Square, finish a combo with Triangle, leap to enemies at middle distance, execute them in single blows from stealth, and perform special attacks that are on cooldowns, with L2 and one of the face buttons. Those special attacks are unlocked over time as you level up - there are only six in total, with minor upgrades to each - as are various other modifying abilities like, say, doing a slishy-slashy attack when you press a button while sprinting. Then there's a separate skill tree, where you can pick a limited number of genetic tweaks at a given moment, unlocked by collecting hidden whiskey bottles found just off the beaten track, that give a sense of very light RPG-ness to things: you can build Wolverine more towards abilities and cooldowns, or to detecting collectibles, or to building and maintaining your rage meter.
Aha - the rage meter! This one's similarly familiar again: you build up rage by attacking enemies, faster by performing a "barrage", which is where you mash Square at a stunned enemy to stab the absolute life out of them. On filling up one bar, your attacks and finishers get more powerful. On two, you start to Hulk Ou– sorry, go full Wolverine, and can now execute basic grunts and damaged foes by pulling both triggers when prompted. Speaking of prompts, there's also a traffic light parry system - blue for parryable attack, red for non-parryable, gold for a "reckless attack" that does a lot of damage to you if you whiff the parry, or a lot of damage to them if you time it right. There's also an ability to smash conveniently-placed molten-hot containers to get "hot claws", which do more damage and make sparks fly with some nice particle physics, but that's about it. And, in fact, that's about it for the combat, frankly.
This is really the core disappointment of Marvel's Wolverine. There's just little to no invention throughout, and nowhere is it felt more prominently than in the fighting, which really has to be the backbone of a linear action game like this, let alone a Wolverine one. Much has been made of the gore - and it is ferociously gory - but that, as with much of the combat, gets old a little too fast. I should emphasise it's not bad: there's all the inherent satisfaction of a good parry-counter, of leaping around fully in character as this unleashed beast, of enacting righteous vengeance on your foes. It's just there's also a sense - that only builds over time - it's all slightly too one-note and one-pace. Wolverine's only settings are yelling and extra yelling, its effects only gory or extra gory, the tone rage or extra rage, the combatants (mostly) only grunts, extra grunts, or bigger grunts. The result is a feeling that you never quite hit the apex of all this action - there's no climax, as we're more or less at maximum rage-against-the-odds throughout.
Meanwhile, after the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh wave of jump-and-parryable-attack guys comes at you with the exact same cadence of parry timing and bullet-dodging you just start to glaze over a little. Ding, ding-ding… ding! Ding, ding-ding… ding! When you're putting your fist through someone's eyes, face, heart and feeling absolutely nothing, it's a sign something's a little off. In the blandest terms: too many of the same enemies, dealt with in the same way, for too long. There are bosses, but probably too few and again too familiar or predictable, given the material on offer. I look to other recent action games - God of War the obvious comparison, but also Insomniac's own in the Marvel's Spider-Man series - and the lack of agency you have as a player, the lack of expressive, inventive, melodramatic or just silly options you had for dealing with problems, is perhaps the true issue. Playing Wolverine I suddenly realised just how important it was that Spider-Man let you ping someone on the bonce with a manhole cover.
And this is the real crux of it with Marvel's Wolverine. The sense I have - I've no evidence for this - is that this is an attempt at doing something a little more efficiently, budget-wise, than the infamously expensive Spider-Man games. They may have come to be a symbol of western triple-A's funding largesse, but they were also a total blast because of it. Wolverine may still be a looker in places, and be perfectly capable of a good old fashioned, quick-time-event-powered set-piece, but it also feels strangely budget by comparison. The collectibles, for instance, feel perhaps aptly like something from a distant and half-remembered gaming past: identikit crates that give you +50 "material" for crafting unlocked suits; whiskey bottles that unlock upgrades; "caches" that are just glowing blue or red non-entities dotted around the place that you whack for XP. Even on the visual side things can feel a little stripped back, just occasionally: not-that-distant backgrounds fade into LOD murkiness, even on PS5 Pro, and NPCs are a little rudimentary. (Though as you'd expect for Sony first-party, there are still glorious looks in places, lots of shiny ray-tracing and sparkles and forearm hair, and it runs smooth as you like).
None of this need be an issue in its own right. Moving to a linear format versus an open world makes total sense, and there's absolutely space for this kind of game. Long live the old-fashioned campaign blockbuster! But with so little invention Wolverine feels like less of a throwback than it does a relic. Memory sequences are - surprise - mostly variations on floating rocks in non-space. Mind-bending enemies quickly transform into meat-n-bones punchbags like the rest. QTEs abound. You look at the linear or linear-like campaigns of recent years, even setting aside the megablockbuster tier of say The Last of Us, and it struggles to compare. Set Marvel's Wolverine against the time-and-space rending movement of Titanfall 2, the lavish ferocity and booming scale of the first modern God of War, the sheer fidelity of recent Call of Duty: Modern Warfares, the cinema of 007: First Light and directorial playfulness of Alan Wake 2, and there just isn't the same spark. Even on the combat front things have evolved again, from the parrying of Sekiro, that makes you feel almost superhuman, to the sheer, bladed speed of, say, Ninja Gaiden 4. My hope is that this doesn't discourage others from having a stab at a linear structure, if you'll pardon the pun. But - oh god, forgive me - this one doesn't quite cut it.
The result, sadly, is a sense that our old boy Wolverine is just caught behind the times. Were it not for the lovability of Logan himself, the animalistic warmth that Insomniac summons through its cast - and the sheer and genuine humanity that can be accessed through that - or the basic pleasure and occasional spectacle its action can offer when spread out into smaller doses, it could've been a bloodbath. Instead, it's just fine. It might be in no small part thanks to the innate nature of the X-Men universe that it's still ultimately enjoyable enough: these stories are all deeply sensitive characters and wearily timely themes. But still, there's still just enough sincerity, character and camp here to keep this old dog alive.
A copy of Marvel's Wolverine was provided for this review by Sony Interactive Entertainment.

item.title: A clone of Old School RuneScape that appeared on the internet this week, and stoked the ire of the RuneScape community, has quickly been shut down. Read more
item.description:
A clone of Old School RuneScape that appeared on the internet this week, and stoked the ire of the RuneScape community, has quickly been shut down.
The clone was made by e OpenAI employee Rohan Varma, who used the GPT-6 Astra to build a version of RuneScape he named Elderwood, which was playable in a browser.
In a video - itself created with gen-AI - uploaded to X, we see a character created and spawning outside Lumbridge castle, with an inventory of bread, coins, and basic tools. We then see the same character fighting giant rats, chopping trees, and equipping steel armour. It looks incredibly similar to Old School RuneScape save for a few inconsistencies..
But as Verma continued to experiment and share their progress on X, the posts caught the attention of the Old School RuneScape community who were displeased with what they found. In a thread posted to the 2007scape Reddit, users were not shy in their criticisms.
"What in the vibe coded shit is this. They even straight up ripped art assets shameless," wrote user RangeCreed. "Love the tweet format. AI bros can only speak in numbers and bullet lists (ideally both at once)," adds Lekamil, while X user Toppo simply summarised the situation with the following: "tl;dr garbage."
The next day, following a spike in players after the aforementioned Reddit post, Elderwood was updated with "lots of content moderation", but also two more areas from RuneScape: Varrock and Falador.
Fast-forward to last night and the game is taken down. In its place, a farewell message that reads as follows: "We received a notice from Jagex asking us to take down the website. Following that notice, we are discontinuing Elderwood's operation, and the game is no longer available.
"Elderwood began as a browser-based multiplayer adventure inspired by RuneScape. In a few short days, it grew into a shared world of exploration, skilling, quests, trading and duels—shaped along the way by the people who showed up to play and share ideas.
"Thank you to everyone who joined us. For the levels earned, the laughs in chat, the suggestions, the patience with bugs, and all the little moments in between: you made this a joy to build and a world worth sharing. "We're keeping the high scores available as a record of what you achieved together."
RuneScape players found this post as well, and scrutinised it. "Why [are] they acting as if they had some glorious adventure and legacy to leave behind lol," wrote user Big_Necessary_5002, the most liked response in the thread.
The community's response is unsurprising. Not only is it rough to see a game you love almost identically copied and regurgitated, but RuneScape players have been suffering the downsides of generative AI for some time now. AI agents can operate bots, potentially worsening a long-term problem the players and devs have been battling against for years.
If you're interested in playing the real RuneScape, Jagex recently released two new quests to Old School. One is an adventure where you talk to crabs and organise a musical number, while the other lets you adopt stray dogs. Sometimes you just can't beat the original.

UPDATE 11TH SEPTEMBER 9.30AM BST: Ubisoft has since made its statement about changing Connect public.
ORIGINAL STORY 10TH SEPTEMBER 3.45PM BST: In a surprise move, Ubisoft announced its intention to remove the need for Ubisoft Connect to start each time you launch one of its games on Steam. Ubisoft Connect, previously known as Uplay, is a store and launcher for Ubisoft's games. It starts when you launch any Ubisoft game you own on Steam or the Epic Games Store.
But starting with Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown, this will no longer be required. Ubisoft explained in a Steam post - only available to owners of the game - it's testing a new "Ubisoft Connect Services Steam Tool" that keeps Connect features like cross-progression, cross-play, rewards "without requiring the Ubisoft Connect PC launcher to be installed or launched".
"This first version is an initial step toward a smoother and more streamlined launch experience on Steam," the publisher reportedly said, as shared by Reddit user NostalgiaKeeper007.
"We will continue to iterate and improve Ubisoft Connect Services over time, with the goal of delivering the features and services players use and expect while making the Steam experience as seamless as possible."
Ubisoft said the same tool "will progressively evolve and roll out to more Ubisoft games on Steam in the future", though it's unclear whether the tool will require future buyers to link their Ubisoft account to Steam - something that's needed today with Connect.
This dual-launcher approach is not unique to Ubisoft, but other publishers, such as EA, don't tend to bundle their launchers with all games they sell on Steam. Usually a lighter, more invisible version starts alongside a game and doesn't noticeably get in the way.
